editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Ewing Rabb Emison, Jr. [March 28, 2003]

div2.p: Interview with Ewing Rabb Emison 1 March 28, 2003 Preface The following oral history testimony is the result of a videotaped interview with Ewing Rabb Emison,

Jr., conducted by (?Interviewer?)on March 28th, 2003, on behalf of the Veterans' Oral History Project. The interview took place in (?Location?), and is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.
The interview was transcribed and processed by Dayette Zampolin.

The reader should bear in mind that she or he is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be read as a personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of place, names, foreign words, and personal names have been verified, either by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably remain regarding some words and their spellings. In these scenarios, a (ph) follows a word or name that is spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: This recording is made March 28th, 2003 with Ewing Rabb Emison, Jr. He goes by the name—Rabb is his first name. 1528 Old Orchard Road in Vincennes, Indiana. Rabb is a native of Vincennes and Knox County, served in the United States Navy. His highest rank attained was that of Lieutenant from 1943 to 1946; and then again, from 1951 to his release in 1952. This recording is made by order from the Office of US Senator Dick Luger. Rabb, thank you for being part of the Veterans History Project.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Well, it's my pleasure.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: You entered the—the military at age 17 and went in the Navy. Now, you were living in Vincennes at that time?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yes, that's right. It was my freshman year in college at DePauw. And I had been in school; and of course, that was the year after Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: And it was the year of the Battle of Midway, and of course, the Battle of Guadalcanal. And so, in school at the age of 17, in September, some of my friends lied about their age and went in, and couldn't go in until they were 18, but some of my high school class had already enlisted.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Rabb, how was the reaction at home to your entering the military?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Oh, nothing at all, I mean, no—no adverse. They --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Everybody—but I mean a lot—every other town in the country, so many young men were—they all going, weren't they?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Oh, yes. It was—nowhere, at that time, was there any adverse position about what we find today. It is amazing the—what should I say, solidified that --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: I tell you, the political program at Vincennes was quite strong. Right?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yes, yes, yes, it was. When I was in high school, there was a symbol put up, V for victory. And so the high school where the—the place where we played basketball had a great big V made out of metal. And down below it, they put the code letter for V, but the school people didn't know the Morse Code. When they—instead of putting three dots and a dash, it was two dots and a dash. I'll remember that. That's the Morse Code for U, and—the letter U. And I can remember sitting there, thinking how funny that was that this school is really anxious to show uniform support for the military service, but they didn't know how to do it.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Yeah. Rabb, where did you go for—well, for enlistment, first of all?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Well, I went over and enlisted in Indianapolis. And about a week later, I got a note for me to return. And I thought, "Good Lord, I just enlisted, and they told me I wouldn't be called till I was 18," but I forgot to put JR on my enlistment paper when I turned in my Birth Certificate. Of course, the very clever person, who used to see that these things were correct, sent me a note, "Come over and add JR." So I had to sit down and say, "JR" on several papers. I remember that. Thought that maybe I had been called up. It didn't—it didn't happen. Not then.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Where was basic training?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Basic training, I didn't have any such thing as basic training. I enlisted as a Naval Aviation Cadet.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Oh?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: And I went down to Kentucky, where there was a pre-flight school. And that's where you, first of all, learned how to put on the Navy uniform.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Which camp was that?

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Okay? You were in Kentucky?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yes. And that was at Murray State. It was then called Murray State, and I don't know what it might be called now.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Still Murray State.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Is it? Okay.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: That was a nice school. That was a nice school. And I can remember—one of the things that I remember was the athletic training they had there. It was pretty intense. And we had a obstacle course, (?something?).
That hadn't been thought of all these years. The obstacle course was running down a lane, and there was a little tiny stream that ran just at the edge of campus.
And to cross that stream, we had to cross on a log.

We've seen these pictures of other people, military, learn how to run across logs over streams. And then to get back to the next time, we had to swing on a rope, kind of like Tarzan. And then, what I thought was the most remarkable thing, the football field was surrounded by a high stone block wall. And we had to learn how to run up the side of that wall, and grab it at the top, and pivot, and go over it. And I used to think how easy it is to get in this football stadium. And maybe I can do this again some day, other places, you know._______ I thought that wall about—I'm going to make it about 12 feet high, something like that, but our physical shape at that time, (?necessarily?) didn't mean anything, we just went over it.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: How was the physical training for you, was it --

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Oh, yes, it was very good. Very good.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Very rigorous?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Rigorous is the word.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Did it reflect war-time conditions, you think?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Ah. To—to answer that question exactly and say war-time, I don't know, but I think it reflected an interest in making sure that the person involved was in the very best physical condition. Yes. Yes. So that's war-time. The answer's yes.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Yes. Well, after that, did you have an initial assignment, out?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Well, we left—well, we were there for three months, and then we went to school at Normal, Illinois, where there was another, it was Illinois, Wesley, it seems to me. And then we got our preliminary aerial training. And I didn't make it through there. They let me—kicked me out of the course, because I failed them, tests. And that's the one thing in life that just grieves me. And as I've lived longer and learned to fly, after I got out, I realized my instructor was not a good instructor. I didn't want to blame it on him --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: —but I'm going to. That I was not instructed correctly. 'Cause I got instruction elsewhere that taught me differently --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: I don't have any details.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Okay. But then I went up to Great Lakes as a discharged Aviation Cadet. And then I got into a program called V-12. After naval aviation was V-5, V not standing for victory or anything like that. It's just a Navy letter. And I got up to Great Lakes, and, lo and behold, they decided to send me off to the college training program, which was V-5, and I went down to South Carolina. And that was not rigorous. It was college training, and then I was there for a year. Got two academic years in one year.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Hm.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: And then I went to, that would be another number V—oh, God, V-1, which is at Abbott Hall. The same Abbott Hall that we heard about earlier this morning. And this was officer training. And we were issued officer uniforms, and made it through that training. And I was then commissioned as an ensign, just like the first witness you had today was commissioned as an ensign.

Then, while I'm there, I was sent to a school I think was remarkable. It was down in Gulf Port. And the Gulf Port training there was in aircraft identification. And we were trained to identify aircraft, to identify targets for our Navy anti-aircraft guns. Because, in the middle of battle, it's difficult for the gunner to pick up targets. And so somebody else has to be there to select them and call them out. And that's what my work was. And then, lo and behold, before we were done, one of the atom bombs were dropped, which ended any war-time training right there. There may have been war-time training going on somewhere else, but --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: What about your output, Rabb, what did you think when you heard the news about that?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: I had a mixture. Of course, I was delighted the war was over. I followed the news. This is before television.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: And you had to read for it—all the news. And I followed the news about battles, and combats. And I was terribly interested in it. And I was a—if I can say this without meaning harm, I was disappointed. I wanted to get out there and participate in it. I learned later that my role on the ship would have been on the bridge.

And the bridge, of course, is where—this just is a command center for a ship. And has—kind of, you know, decks outside the door of the bridge where the fire control director, which would have been me, but I still thought, "Gee, it would have been great to have been out there," but the kamikazes, the suicide planes, dove right for that bridge. That was their favorite target. I read about that later. I was—as a greenling, I was disappointed that I didn't get to see any—of all things to be disappointed about, didn't get to see any combat time; but if I'd gone out there at that—you know, the bomb had not—atom bomb had not dropped, if I'd have gone out there, I'd have found myself at the center of the target, each time. So I learned to have a different attitude about it. Oh... One of the books that I've read that use, oh, gee whiz, continued—Paul Fussel was an infantry officer who fought in Europe, was injured, and was sent out the Pacific with his company to land in Japan. He wrote a book with the crudest title, "Thank God for the atom bomb." And the point he was making was, that saved a lot of lives. It cost a lot of lives. Saved a lot of lives. I've just in the last two days had not prepared for his interview—but during the ______ of the last few days, I read a story about what President Truman did to help decide what to do with the atom bomb. And the theory at the time was that the invasion might cost as much as 500,000 lives.
Well, I think mine would have been one of them. And—all right. 500,000 lives versus 100,000, whatever...
The atom bomb. And Truman made the decision. I never was a big fan of Truman's, but it was said about him, you know, on his desk was a little rock, and written on it,

"The buck stops here." And I think he's that kind of a guy. He made that decision. Tough, tough decision. So my—well—well, my first opinion about the atom bomb was disappointment that I wouldn't get to participate in any exciting combat, but I got older and smarter, and I learned to be pleased that I didn't have to. It belonged to other people.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Well, Rabb, you were part of that enormous US effort --

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: —nonetheless. And what does it—what are the lessons of World War II that maybe, 50 years from now, some future generation might need to know about?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Mmm, boy. That's a nice question, and I wish I had a day or so to answer it. In all the three years, I only heard one comment of criticism about the war. And it was in a barber shop. Somebody that—well, they didn't like something, or they—I don't know what it was. But in that period of time, everybody had to contribute. I mean, gasoline was rationed, food was rationed. They were very calm and cagey when the family would lose a relative. And although there's sadness for that family,

I can't characterize all of them the same; but nevertheless, they felt it was at a good cause. It was some mistakes made in World War II, as you know, as internment of Japanese citizens in California, and isolation of black people, putting them in separate places and—in the military camps.
[Interview interrupted by phone call.)

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: But the movies that were put out then for public consumption could give some idea. I don't mean it's a bitter time in the United States. I'll bet this.

There must have been uniform-identity or similarity. One of the movies I remember, so silly, America have good—what shall I say? European appearance. Had its face made over to look like a Japanese, and so he could go in and entreat upon the Japanese. What a nutty attitude?

But that was characteristic, I think, of the times that would show what a person would do, of course, no person was reported doing that, but oh, there were a lot of sacrifices people made, which you don't find today. I hitchhiked everywhere. Everybody had—not everybody, but chiefly enlisted men. I was down in South Carolina, and I hitchhiked all my life. And it was a—it was—it was—this was something Jack Johnson never did. I listened to him. He was a college graduate when he started, but to be just a rookie, he'd go out to the edge of town, and there would be a string of soldiers or string of servicemen standing there, trying to get a ride. And it was improper to go to the head of the line. You went to the back of the line, knowing that the person who was at the head of the line would picked up first. And there's no written rule on that, but that was characteristic. And I was picked up in all kinds of equipment, and I learned a lot and enjoyed a lot. So my—my period in those three years before—I went over to the Philippines, and we'll talk about that in a minute, but I'm going to make it two years, my two years being in the country in a Navy uniform pleased me a lot.
Pleased me _____.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: There is something special about the Navy, isn't there?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Well, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: There is a special comradery?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: There is. There is.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: And I keep hearing that. And I keep hearing this immense loyalty to ship?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes, indeed, yes, indeed. Here's one thing that I can't demonstrate right now. You know, there were four ships named Vincennes. The very first one, I have a picture in the next room. The very first one was a survey ship, sailing vessel, that's sailing round. The next ship was a heavy cruiser that was lost in the Battle of Savo Island. That's 1942, when the battle down in Guadalcanal went on. The Japanese—we thought we were taught to be—be quicker about them, but they were good fighters, they had good ships, and they were good at their nighttime fighting. They sunk the Vincennes at night. There was a third Vincennes that finished the war. And I think it was finished at—I'm not sure, but at Bikini. By that I mean an island, atoll in the Pacific, where atom bombs were dropped on ships. I think it ended there. I'm not sure. There is a fourth Vincennes, and it is now active. And in this little city for the last at least 30 years, it may be more than that, we've had annual reunions of Vincennes veterans. And my regret is, I didn't go to those meetings, because there were people who would show up, who would board the Vincennes that sunk at Savo Island, and they would come here. And to my surprise there were some men who moved here because of the way they were received here. They moved the family here to live. Now, you don't find Navy-non-Navy bonding everywhere like you do here. And that's unusual about this town; but there is, you know, at City Hall, a room of Vincennes artifacts from a ship or the ship. Plural. And then being bonded to the ship on which you serve, I can't explain it, except, that ship is a moving vessel. And so you live in different cities, you visit different locations. And you visit them with the same crew, you know. And so you have memories that are similar. What it's like to be in Buenos Aires, what it's like to be in Johannesburg. One of the stories I remember, and God bless this guy, the Marblehead was an ancient cruiser.
And it was over there in the Philippines when the war started. And it was attacked. And it was badly damaged.

A lot of people were killed. And when the Marblehead got out, it managed to survive, and it got out of Philippines area and got south down next—we're talking about the heat of the battle, got down to Australia. This is the story of a man who was a boarder, a boarder. He was an officer, and they sailed that Marblehead across the Indian Ocean, around South Africa, up the Atlantic to Boston, which was her home port. And there were so many people who had been lost and killed, that the officers' duties, that were going on, was four hours on, four hours off. That's—you just couldn't get eight hours off, because you didn't have enough men.

And the ship's rudder, the steering mechanism, was destroyed. And they steered it by using the different screws at the stern. Advance this engine, advance that engine. And they sailed that vessel, they say, around Africa, up the Atlantic. And would you believe those people are bonded? You bet they are or were. They're gone now. Most of them are gone. But that happens in any ship that's been in battle. That, ha, you know that they're bonded. That's why, you think of it, in modern times, I'm talking about since World War II, three ships named Vincennes, of course, in the different battles, different events, but they're—they're bonded.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Common --

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: —bond.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: That's one thing that they have.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Rabb, I went to that banquet last year. And you could absolutely feel the love in the room. You really could?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yeah. Well, the numbers are decreasing from what they used to be. It's peace-time duty now for them. And in all of this, some of it, still they're conscious of it, the guys who fought in it, are—you know, the number's decreasing.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Now, you went back in. Right?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yes, well, I want to say, before that—finish here.
I went to the Philippines --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: —and I spent there a—year. And I didn't have any (?Blayhelution?)duty like those(?tramp?)or --

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: What ship are you on, going out there?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Oh, it was a troop ship.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: And I was sent out there for a duty in the Philippines. And I sailed it, some little unit called the Phillipine Seafront there. And the purpose I was there was just—we—we kept—the United States kept military people out there for a year, not sure what Russia's going to do. And I know what I'd have done if the Russians did anything, but I was out there for a year. And one day, my one story to tell, about my memory there. I was just a rookie officer. And one day, the --
I was in the—a section of—ashore. "On the beach."
We used to say, "On the beach," called, "Operations."
And my top officer in Operations was a Captain Reynolds.

Little guy, just tough as nails, Academy man. And he sent me out to the harbor. He said, "There's a sailing ship out there called the Lanakai. Go out and see if it's there." So I—"Okay," got a Jeep and drove out there. I had some binoculars with me, and I went down,
"Yeah, there's a sailing ship," and I read on the stern,
"Lanakai." "And why the hell do they want to know about this?" So I went back and put the binoculars away and told the captain, "Yes, the Lanakai is out there."
"Okay. That's all," and he went and did something else.

Now, I want to tell you, that as Pearl Harbor approached, and we're not supposed to—records say we didn't know anything about it. Well, as December 7th had—well, about December 1, end of November, December 1, 1941, President Roosevelt sends a message to Manila, and says, "Send a disguised ship out west from Manila, because the Japanese are coming down, and they're coming to Indochina to take that over, you know,

_____+____+_____ China." And the ship that went over there was run by a Navy Lieutenant whose name was—I'm going to guess at this, Droop, D-r-o-o-p, is the way I remember it, but not quite right. And a couple of Navy Officers and a lot of native Filipinos. And now, I don't know what it was that it hadn't gotten out very far when Pearl Harbor happened until it was called back.

The ship was the Lanakai. And that man who was a skipper, a lieutenant, later, he just died a little while ago, '91 or '92. That he wrote several books about his experience, because he believes that President Roosevelt, now, this may not be fair, sent him out as a target ship for the Japanese. That there was no purpose in him being out there in that ship. That there are other ways of finding out what the Japanese were doing.
That's the—the opinion of that particular officer.

So, my similar experience I remember the most about being in the Philippines is, I'd looked at that ship, and there, this is now, in 1946, five years later—not five, I'm going to make it four and a half. Something like that. From that experience there, "Who owned that ship? What's it doing there?" And I want to know more about it. But here it is 2003, and that ship is no more.

So I'll never know that bit of mystery. Now, Jack told—Jack Johnson, I told you this morning that he saw me in the Philippines. What happened is that Jack was on his way home after his August period out there.

And, yeah, it was a staging area. By staging area is where officers came in and officers went out. And I just ran into him. That was an outdoor movies with just benches in the side of a hill. And there is Johnson. My gosh, I couldn't believe it. And the story of the rest of that is correct. I told him how to be the first ones there to get a cold beer after the movie, except I was running down a hill steeply, and there was this bush in front of me, and I just go on running right through the bush, but it was a big coral stone and had vine over it.

And that ended my rush for the cold beer. Johnson was behind me somewhere. He didn't admit that he had, but he had anyway, so we did meet over there. He was on his way home, and I was on my way out. And that tells the story of the difference of our experiences. The second time I was called was not terribly exciting. I was just really surprised. Okay. I never did get discharged. I felt a duty to the Navy, because they gave me a college education while I was in the Navy. They didn't give me a good one, but they gave me one. And I get this notice to report to the Brooklyn Army Base in—in Brooklyn.

Oh. I had, when I was in the Philippines, incurred hepatitis. And I think that was from some bad food or something I had. And I was in—in sickbay. That's what the Navy calls their hospital. Sickbay. Pleasant doctor comes by, and he says, "You're going to get a medical discharge. You're in no shape ..." Okay. The next thing I know, the doctor's sent home. And I don't get any medical discharge. And, a matter of fact, I don't—as I've told you, I don't get any discharge at all. So here I am, called up again, and I say, when I go out there, I say, "You know, my last days, or not quite my last days in the Philippines, I still had hepatitis and was not in satisfactory physical condition." "Oh," says this lawyer who—lawyer—doc—not doctor, this officer who's receiving me, "Well, I tell you, you go ahead and sign in, and we'll check on it." I had a report, showing what my condition was, showing I was not satisfactory.
"And we'll check this out." Well, I signed in, I'm now a Navy officer again. And I come back, and the guy who told me to sign it says, "You're right." He says,

"You're not in a good physical condition." "And what am I doing here?" "Well," he says, "Well, you just stay in." So I stayed in. And what I did there was be on the staff. And we shipped troops to Korea. And what this particular station did, weren't very many, but we leased private troop ships. We sent people to Korea or brought them back. So ... And it was—it was not very exciting, but that's what I did for a year and a half.
And then I came home. And then, as I mentioned earlier,

I enlisted in '42 and was called back in '52. And in '62, I get this news from the Navy, says, "When you get your next notice, you'll report to the Post Office in Saint Louis," just where I'm going to report. And I just can't believe it. I can't believe it. And I should have saved that little notice. If I had known we were going to be sitting here today, I would have saved that notice as a display; but, you know, I carried it in my wallet for two or three years. "Well, they're not going to call me," so I threw it away. But at this moment, which is March 28th, 2003, I have not been discharged from my 1942 enlistment in the Navy. And I'll bet I hold the record for the longest—longest, what shall I say?
Career in the Navy, not career time, but I mean being enlisted. Maybe I can't say being enlisted, maybe I'm not enlisted. There just is many ways of seeing it ...

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: You never got the paperwork. Right?______.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: No. No. I've been several times. And now I don't care. What's there to care about? I'm sure that my days will end, and I'm a Navy member. And that's all right.
That's all right.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Die a Navy man?

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: That's all right. That's okay.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: Rabb, thank you.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Larry Ordner
sp.p: It's been a pleasure.

sp.speaker: Ewing R. Emison
sp.p: Okay. I'm sorry my report was not as exciting as --
